chapter_en: The Blessings over Fruits and Shehakol

sections.title_en: Fruits of the Tree and of the Ground
sections.body_en:
Over fruits of the tree one recites "Borei peri ha-etz" ("who creates the fruit of the tree"), and over fruits of the ground one recites "Borei peri ha-adama" ("who creates the fruit of the ground"). For example, over grapes, pomegranates, apples, pears, walnuts and almonds – one recites Ha-etz; and over corn, lentils, peas, tomatoes and cucumbers – one recites Ha-adama.

A fruit of the ground grows quickly. Within a few months of its sowing or planting it yields fruit, and the simple power of the ground is more evident in it. In contrast, a fruit of the tree undergoes a complex process: in the first years the tree must grow and take shape; afterwards, in a relatively long process, it absorbs nourishment from the ground, digests it and grows its fruits. One can say that a fruit of the ground expresses basicness and simplicity, whereas a fruit of the tree expresses refinement and complexity, and generally its taste too is deeper and richer.

The tree resembles man; both must undergo a prolonged process until they reach maturity, but afterwards their fruits are superior. And like the tree, whose fruits of the first three years are forbidden to eat under the law of orla, so too man must learn Torah and be educated in the mitzvot before he begins to act in the world.

Originally, it was fitting for man to eat only fruits of the tree, as it is stated (Bereishit 2:16): "Of every tree of the garden you may freely eat." And even grain, which is man's main food, used to grow on a tree, and according to Rabbi Yehuda, the Tree of Knowledge was wheat (Berakhot 40a). In contrast, the animals were meant to eat fruits of the ground and grasses. After the sin, man fell from his level, and in order to repair himself he needed the fruits of the ground, for simpler and more basic repairs. And grain too fell with him and became a grass. And man was charged to toil and labor in order to produce his food from the ground – to plow, sow, reap, grind, knead and bake – as it is stated (Bereishit 3:19): "By the sweat of your brow shall you eat bread, until you return to the ground." Through this toil man repairs his bad character traits, and in a long and prolonged process prepares himself and the world for redemption.

And although man's main food now comes from the fruits of the ground, the fruits of the tree still have tremendous importance, for they elevate and enhance the quality of his life, and connect him to a higher level. And in the future, after the world is repaired, man's food will once again be fruit of the tree, and there will be no toil in sowing it every year, as the Sages said (Ketubot 111b): "In the future wheat will rise as tall as a palm tree … Lest you say there will be difficulty in reaping it (because of the height of the palm) … the Holy One, blessed be He, will bring a wind from His storehouses and blow upon it, and it will shed its fine flour, and a person will go out to the field and bring back a handful, and from it will be his livelihood and the livelihood of his household." And regarding the Land of Israel they said: "In the future the Land of Israel will produce gluskaot (ready-made cakes) and garments of fine wool (beautiful clothes)" (see Pri Tzadik, Tu Bi-Shevat 1).

Thus fruit of the tree has a special virtue, and fruit of the ground too has its own importance, and for each of them one must thank God with the wording of the blessing particular to it. Through the blessing, the inner virtue of the fruit is actualized, and the holy spark within it is revealed and adds blessing to a person's life.

sections.title_en: Between Fruit of the Ground and Fruit of the Tree
sections.body_en:
If one erred and recited "Borei peri ha-adama" over a fruit of the tree, he has fulfilled his obligation, because the tree too grows from the ground, so it turns out that he did not say anything false in his blessing. But if one erred and recited "Borei peri ha-etz" over a fruit of the ground, he has not fulfilled his obligation, because the fruit of the ground did not grow on a tree, so it turns out that he did not say a fitting blessing, and he must recite Ha-adama again. Therefore, when there is a doubt about a fruit, whether it is a fruit of the ground or of the tree, one recites Ha-adama (SA 206:1).

A tree has a trunk that endures for many years, and from it grow branches, and on them fruits. And even if it is low and we call it a bush, since its trunk endures from year to year it is considered a tree. For example, over blueberries one recites Ha-etz, since they grow on bushes whose trunks and branches endure for years. And over the fruits of a plant that must be sown or planted every year, one recites Ha-adama.

Regarding perennial plants such as bananas and pineapple, a doubt arose. On the one hand, at the end of each season their trunk withers completely, like fruits of the ground; on the other hand, there is no need to sow them every year, for they regrow from their roots, and they also rise to a height of four meters like large trees. In halakha, since their trunk does not endure, their blessing is Ha-adama (SA 203:2-3). Regarding papaya too a doubt arose, for although the papaya trunk endures for several years, it is hollow like a thick stalk, and already in its first year it yields fruit like a vegetable. Since this is so, over papaya fruit too one recites Ha-adama. Likewise over raspberries and blackberries one recites Ha-adama, because every year they put out new branches from the ground, which yield fruit in their second year and then wither. Therefore there is also no prohibition of orla on them.1

notes_en.en: Berakhot 40b: "Wherever, when you take the fruit, the gavza (stem) does not remain to produce again (when its fruits are picked, there is no gavza that afterwards produces fruit again) – we do not recite over it Borei peri ha-etz but rather Borei peri ha-adama." In Peninei Halakha: Kashrut 2:8, notes 12-13, it is cited that admittedly some hold that the Rishonim disagreed about the definition of gavza, and consequently, in their view, a disagreement arises regarding orla and blessings for several species. However, in halakha and in practice, it seems that all agree that a tree is a plant that has a trunk and roots that endure and grow stronger from year to year, and by virtue of this their fruits multiply from year to year; therefore over caper one recites Ha-etz even though sometimes all its branches wither from year to year, since its trunk grows stronger from year to year. Conversely, it is understandable why one recites Ha-adama over bananas, eggplants, peppers, papaya and passion fruit, and likewise they do not have the law of orla, since their trunk does not grow stronger from year to year but is either newly formed or weakens. As for raspberries and blackberries, it is clear that they are species that grow for two years at most, and therefore their law is like fruit of the ground, as explained there in note 13.

sections.title_en: Over What Does One Recite Shehakol?
sections.body_en:
Over foods that do not grow from the earth, such as the meat of domesticated animals, wild animals, fowl and fish, and likewise over eggs, milk and cheese, the Sages instituted reciting "Shehakol nihya bi-dvaro" ("by whose word all things came to be"). Likewise, one who drinks water to quench his thirst recites Shehakol. Likewise over mushrooms one recites Shehakol, and although they look like fruits of the ground, since they do not draw their nourishment from the ground, their blessing is Shehakol (SA 204:1).

Likewise over wild fruits and leaves that are fit to eat under pressing circumstances one recites Shehakol, and although they grew on a tree or from the ground, since these species are not planted in order to eat them, they do not have the importance of fruit, and their blessing is Shehakol (as explained below in section 6).

Likewise over fruit juices, such as orange juice and apple juice, one recites Shehakol, and although the juice came out of the fruit, since it has changed so much that the food has turned into a drink, its blessing is Shehakol (below, section 15). Likewise over beer made from barley, or coffee and tea, whose taste is produced from plants or fruits, since they have become drinks, their blessing is Shehakol (below, section 17).

Likewise one who eats foods that have spoiled but are still fit to eat under pressing circumstances, such as bread that has become moldy, or a cooked dish whose form has changed and spoiled, recites Shehakol. But if they spoiled completely so that they are not fit for human consumption, one does not recite a blessing over them (SA 204:1; MB 1-2).

Likewise fruits that are usually eaten cooked, such as squash and potatoes, if one ate them raw – he recites Shehakol (SA 205:1; below, section 14).

In general, one can say that the Shehakol blessing was instituted for two types of foods: first, important foods whose source is animal – meat, dairy products and eggs, and likewise mushrooms, whose nourishment is drawn from the air. Second, foods that have changed from their nature to the point that they lost their original blessing, such as foods that turned into a drink, and foods that spoiled but are still edible under pressure. Likewise produce that did not reach the importance of fruit, such as wild fruits. A considerable portion of the halakhic discussions in this chapter deals with the question of at what stage a food changes and loses its original blessing for the Shehakol blessing.

sections.title_en: The Meaning of the Shehakol Blessing and the Law in Case of Doubt
sections.body_en:
Since the Shehakol blessing contains general praise, it can exempt all kinds of foods, so that if one erred and recited Shehakol over a fruit of the tree or a fruit of the ground, or even over bread or Mezonot or wine – he has fulfilled his obligation. However, ideally one should recite over each and every kind its fitting blessing. Only when there is a doubt about a certain food whether its blessing is Shehakol or another blessing does one recite Shehakol in order to get out of the doubt (SA 204:13; 206:1).

When there is a doubt about a fruit, whether its blessing is Ha-etz or Ha-adama, one recites Ha-adama (above, section 2). And although even if we recite Shehakol over it we would fulfill our obligation, it is preferable to recite Ha-adama, which is a more specific blessing that expresses the fact that it is a fruit.

Everything we have learned, that in a case of doubt one recites Shehakol or Ha-adama, applies only where there is no one to ask, or where it is a doubt that has not been decided in halakha. But when it is possible to ask a Torah scholar what the fitting blessing is, it is forbidden to recite Shehakol or Ha-adama out of doubt; rather, one is obligated to clarify which blessing must be recited (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 202:24; MB 202:84).

As a rule, there is a preference for saying a special blessing for each type of food, for each type of food grants a person unique benefit and enjoyment, and if one were to recite a blessing over all types in a uniform and generic way, he would not give expression to the abundance of blessing that God has bestowed upon the world. On the other hand, if one were to recite over a peach a blessing of its own and over an orange a blessing of its own, and so for each and every kind, he would not grasp the general aim of the Holy One, blessed be He, in His world, but would be sunk in the minute details of the material world. Through the institution of blessings for the different types of foods, there is on the one hand expression of the differentiation of the Divine blessing, and on the other hand expression of the general aim. The Shehakol blessing is the blessing that has remained as more representative of the general matter. On the one hand it is not specific, and therefore its stature is lower, and whenever possible one must recite a specific blessing. But on the other hand, it expresses the general idea "that all things came to be by His word." And precisely in it there is an emphasis on the spiritual source of creation, that through speech the Holy One, blessed be He, created His world; for the more one encounters the general, unifying aspect of creation, the more one grasps its spiritual root.

Because of the importance of fruits of the tree and fruits of the ground, the Sages instituted special blessings for them; but for other things that grow on trees and bushes they did not institute a special blessing, and consequently, if they are fit to eat, their blessing is Shehakol. Therefore, one who wishes to eat leaves and stalks of a tree or of an annual plant, such as the tender stalks of a vine or of grain – recites Shehakol (SA 204:1).2

Peels of fruit that are usually eaten together with the fruit, such as the peel of apples, pears and cucumbers, are considered an inseparable part of the fruit, and therefore even one who eats them by themselves recites over them the blessing of the fruit: over cucumber peels Ha-adama, and over apple and pear peels Ha-etz. But over peels that are not usually eaten, such as orange peels, if they were sweetened with sugar or chocolate, one recites Shehakol, for since they are usually thrown away, they are not considered part of the fruit (MB 202:39).

One who eats fresh pods of legumes, such as green bean pods: if he eats them with the beans, he recites Ha-adama over the beans and exempts the pod. And if he eats the pod by itself – he should recite Shehakol (MB 204:9).

Over fruit seeds that are fit to eat one recites Shehakol, because they are not the main part of the fruit. But when they are eaten together with the fruit, they are secondary to the fruit and the blessing over the fruit exempts them.

But over black sunflower seeds one recites Ha-adama, because they are the main part of the fruit. Likewise over (white) pumpkin seeds and over watermelon seeds one recites Ha-adama, because they are grown from special varieties whose flesh is scant and whose seeds are abundant, and they are planted mainly for the seeds; since they are the main part of the fruit, their blessing is Ha-adama (see SA 202:3 and MB there).

notes_en.en:
Whatever is usually eaten and for whose sake too the tree is planted, but does not belong to the main fruit, descends from the level of the Ha-etz blessing to the Ha-adama blessing, as we learned regarding the shoots and peels of the caper (Berakhot 36a; SA 202:6). And if it is something that is not thought of at the time of planting, even though it can be eaten, its blessing is Shehakol. Regarding the cashew nut, which grows on a tree, some initially wished to say that its blessing is Ha-adama, because the cashew nut grows at the tip of the fruit of that tree, and since it is not the main fruit, its blessing is Ha-adama. But in truth, since the tree is grown mainly for the sake of the cashew nut, it is considered the main fruit and its blessing is Ha-etz.
Over kora, which is today called hearts of palm, which grows at the top of the trunks of palms called palmito, one recites Shehakol, because the tree is not planted for its sake. On the contrary, cutting it damages the tree's growth (SA 204:1; MB 9). However, today special palms are grown for hearts of palm. These palms put out many shoots, which are cut in a controlled manner so that the palm continues to grow and produce additional hearts, and therefore their blessing is Ha-adama (and not Peri Ha-etz, since it is not a fruit, as cited in the Behag regarding sugarcane, cited in BHL 202:15, s.v. "al").

sections.title_en: Unripe Fruits, Wild Fruits and Sugarcane
sections.body_en:
Fruits whose taste is sour but which can be eaten under pressing circumstances – if they grew and ripened in their normal way – one recites their own blessing over them. And if their taste is sour because they are still unripe (boser) – the poskim disagreed whether one may recite their own blessing over them, and therefore it is better to recite Shehakol over them.

Over fruits that grow on non-fruit-bearing (wild) trees and are not so tasty, such as small apples and small pears that grow on wild trees, even though they are fit to eat under pressing circumstances, since the trees were not planted for this purpose, they have no importance, and one who eats them recites Shehakol. And even if he cooked them and they became tasty, since the trees were not planted in order to grow fruit, their fruits have no importance, and their blessing is Shehakol (SA 203:4-5). Likewise over stalks that have a certain taste and grow wild, one recites Shehakol (SA 204:1). But over tasty fruits, even if they grew on wild trees, one recites Ha-etz (MB 203:5; 204:18-19). Therefore over the prickly pear (sabras), which is tasty, one recites Ha-etz (Kaf Ha-ḥayim 202:6). Likewise over tasty nuts that grow on wild trees one recites Ha-etz.

Over sucking sugarcane one recites Shehakol; and although the canes grow from the ground, and therefore some hold that their blessing is Ha-adama, since one does not eat the canes themselves but only sucks flavor from them, their blessing is Shehakol (SA 202:15; MB 76).

sections.title_en: Vegetables and Fruits Grown in a Pot and in Water
sections.body_en:
Over a fruit of the ground that grew in a pot without a hole, one recites Ha-adama, even though its roots are not connected to the ground, since what grows there is a kind of soil; in addition, the pot itself also contains soil.

Some are in doubt regarding leaves and fruits of the ground that grew in water without soil, that perhaps, since their roots do not penetrate the ground, it is not right to recite Ha-adama over them, and therefore they ruled that it is preferable to recite Shehakol over them (Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach). However, in practice, since they are plants that are usually grown in the ground, and the very source of these plants and fruits is in plants and fruits that grew in the ground, their blessing is Ha-adama (Or Le-Tzion vol. 2, 14:13; Rav Eliyahu; Shevet Ha-Levi 1:205).

But regarding sprouts, which are known to grow on water, a doubt arose: perhaps their blessing is Ha-adama, since in their growth they resemble fruits of the ground, and perhaps their blessing is Shehakol, since they are not usually grown in the ground. Because of the doubt, it is proper to recite Shehakol over them.

Fruits that were cut or squashed retain their original blessing. For example, one who cuts vegetables for a salad recites Ha-adama, and likewise one who grates a carrot with a grater recites Ha-adama. And if one did this with apples, he recites Ha-etz. Likewise one who mashes a banana recites Ha-adama over it.

If the fruit was completely mashed, the poskim disagreed whether its blessing changed. Some say that although the form of the fruit changed completely, since in practice it is the same fruit that remains, its original blessing remains (Rambam). And some say that since it has changed so much that in people's eyes it is no longer considered a fruit, its blessing is Shehakol (Terumat Ha-deshen). And this is the practice.

In summary, if the fruit was completely mashed its blessing is Shehakol, and if it was not completely mashed its blessing remains as before. However, since the law depends on people's perception, there are exceptions to the rule: sometimes, although it was completely mashed, since it is a fruit that is always mashed, even after its mashing it is still considered a fruit in people's eyes, and consequently one recites the fruit's blessing over it. And sometimes the fruit was not completely mashed, but in people's eyes it changed greatly, and therefore, although it was not completely mashed – its blessing is Shehakol.3

In the following sections we will continue to clarify this law; but first let us state at the outset that in practice there is not so much concern of error here, because if one recited Ha-etz over fruits that were completely mashed – he has fulfilled his obligation, for he did not say anything false in his blessing, since this puree is indeed a product of the fruit of the tree. Likewise, if one recited Shehakol over fruits that were not completely mashed – he has fulfilled his obligation, for in halakha even if one recited Shehakol over a whole fruit – he has fulfilled his obligation (SA 206:1; MB 3). Moreover, the types of foods, the manner of their mashing, and people's perception often change from place to place and from time to time. Therefore one need not be so concerned about these questions, and in a case of doubt the one reciting the blessing may judge for himself: if the identity of the original fruit is still evident in the puree, he should recite its original blessing, and if it has changed greatly – he should recite Shehakol.4

notes_en.en:
The basis of the discussion is in Berakhot 38a, in the law of terima – dates that were squashed, whose blessing is Ha-etz. According to Terumat Ha-deshen 29 and other Rishonim, if they were mashed their blessing is Shehakol, and according to the Rambam and other Rishonim, even when they were completely mashed their blessing is Ha-etz, and only when they became like liquids, which are drunk because of the extent of the mashing, is their blessing Shehakol. There are further shades of opinion in this regarding the definition of complete and incomplete mashing, and some say that there is no disagreement here (Taz; Arukh Ha-shulḥan); I have written the main opinions. The law of cut vegetables is explained in Berakhot 39a, that their blessing is still Ha-adama. Seemingly there is support for the Rambam from Berakhot 36b, from the law of homalta, which is spices crushed in honey, whose blessing remains as before, Ha-adama (and so wrote SA 203:7). However, Terumat Ha-deshen and those who agree with him explain that since they are usually eaten crushed, the crushing does not change their blessing. So too wrote MB 202:44 and BHL 203:6.
It seems to my humble opinion that the root of their disagreement is that according to the Rambam, in every case, mashing does not change the essence of the fruit, and its blessing remains as before. But according to Terumat Ha-deshen and those who agree with him, everything depends on people's perception, and generally, after complete mashing, the puree is no longer considered a fruit but a new food, and therefore its blessing is Shehakol. But if it is a fruit that is usually eaten mashed, and even after it was completely mashed and its form changed people consider it a fruit – its blessing remains as before, for it is not the mashing that determines but people's perception. (And see BHL 202:15, that the blessing over sugar is according to what is visible to the eye.)
And although SA 202:7 ruled like the Rambam, that with any mashing the blessing remains as before, and it seems that this is the opinion of most Rishonim, the Jewish people became accustomed to follow the opinion of Terumat Ha-deshen, that if the mashing changed the form of the fruit, one recites Shehakol over it, for this is people's perception. And perhaps they were also concerned about error in the blessing, for if the food changed greatly, there is no certain knowledge of what it is composed of, and therefore they became accustomed to recite Shehakol over it. So too wrote Rema 202:7, that it is good to take into account the opinion of Terumat Ha-deshen. And so wrote most Aḥaronim in practice. They disagreed how far one should be concerned regarding mashing: according to MA and other Aḥaronim, only with complete mashing that changes its form entirely does one recite Shehakol, and according to Knesset Ha-gedola and other Aḥaronim, even with complete mashing that does not change its form entirely one recites Shehakol. MB 202:42 and BHL, s.v. "temarim," decided in accordance with MA, because one should add the opinion of the Rambam, according to whom it would have been possible according to the basic law to rule; therefore, when its form has not changed so much, one recites over it, as before, Ha-etz or Ha-adama. And this is the custom for Sephardim and Ashkenazim. Admittedly, Yabia Omer 7:29 ruled like SA, but many of the great Sephardic poskim ruled like Terumat Ha-deshen and Rema; so wrote Rav Pe'alim 2:28; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 202:57; Or Le-Tzion 14:2.
Piskei Teshuvot 202:15 summarized several rules from the words of the Aḥaronim: 1) that if it was cooked and mashed its blessing is Shehakol (from MA); 2) that if another species was mixed into it its blessing is Shehakol (from Pri Megadim); 3) that if it was mashed in a special mashing utensil its blessing is Shehakol (from Nahar Shalom). He added several more rules there. But as I wrote, the approach of Terumat Ha-deshen (which is our custom) is to follow people's perception: if this puree is perceived as the same fruit, its blessing remains as before, and if it is no longer perceived as fruit, because it changed greatly, its blessing is Shehakol. All the definitions and rules that the Aḥaronim established are meant to assist in deciding, but they do not change the foundation, that everything depends on people's perception. And since the matter depends on people's perception, opinions on it are many, for there are borderline situations. If we examine our custom in all the blessings over mashed fruits, we will find that no single rule stands on its own against the test of the blessings we customarily recite. And sometimes it appears that there is a disagreement among the Aḥaronim, but in truth they spoke about different places and different eating habits. Therefore we must follow what is accepted in the perception of most people, and this is in practice what most poskim ruled.

We learned in SA 206:1 that over all species, if one recited Shehakol he has fulfilled his obligation. Likewise the reverse: if one recited Ha-etz over a fruit that was mashed so much that its form changed completely – he has fulfilled his obligation, because there is nothing false in his words, as MA 206:1 wrote regarding a similar case, and the vast majority of Aḥaronim agreed with him, among them Birkei Yosef 206:2, Ḥayei Adam 51:12, and MB 206:3. Yabia Omer vol. 7, 29:9, elaborated on this. And although some disagreed with this, the halakha follows the majority. Furthermore, according to the Rambam and those who agree with him, in every case its blessing remains as before. Therefore, where the law is not known, the one reciting the blessing may decide according to what he sees.
When a person remains in an evenly balanced doubt – he should recite Shehakol, as Rema 202:7 wrote, and as the Beit Yosef 202:15 wrote regarding the blessing over sugar, and this is the opinion of most Aḥaronim. For the Shehakol blessing, according to its plain meaning, can apply to all species, whereas the Ha-etz blessing applies to a species that has changed only by way of interpretation. (This is not as Yabia Omer wrote, that the halakha follows the Rambam and it is preferable to recite a specific blessing.)

sections.title_en: Fruits That Were Not Completely Mashed and Retain Their Blessing
sections.body_en:
Over dates that were squashed and became like a paste, one recites Ha-etz, and at the end one Me'ein Shalosh blessing. For since they were not completely mashed, they did not lose their form and appearance entirely, and their blessing remains as before.5

Over avocado that was mashed, since it was not completely mashed and its special texture remains, one recites Ha-etz. And even if onion and lemon were added to it for flavor, since it did not change so much and everyone relates to it as avocado, its blessing is Ha-etz.

Over eggplant salad made of mashed eggplants with mayonnaise, since it is not completely mashed, if one wishes to eat it by itself, one recites Ha-adama.

Over levivot (latkes) made of grated potato (on a grater), since the potato was not completely mashed, one recites Ha-adama. But over levivot made of potato flour, since it was completely mashed, and it is not so evident what it was made from, one recites Shehakol. Likewise over potato kugel: if pieces of potato are discernible in it, one recites Ha-adama, and if they are not discernible – Shehakol.

Sometimes a fruit is cut into slices and its form is changed by drying or frying, such as thin slices of dried apple; since the fruit did not undergo mashing, its blessing does not change.6

notes_en.en: So wrote MB 202:42 and Yabia Omer vol. 7, 20 [?], paragraphs 4, 10, 14. And if the mashing completely changed the appearance and form of a fruit of the seven species, so that it is not discernible which fruit it is, then even though it was ruled at the outset that one should recite Shehakol, if one ate a kezayit of it a doubt arises regarding the after-blessing: according to the Rambam its blessing is Me'ein Shalosh – Al Ha-etz, and according to Terumat Ha-deshen its blessing is Borei Nefashot. In halakha, MB 202:42 wrote that one should recite Al Ha-etz, because most Rishonim hold like the Rambam, and only because of the doubt did most Aḥaronim write like Terumat Ha-deshen. Admittedly, Kaf Ha-ḥayim 57 wrote that one should recite Borei Nefashot; however, since according to most poskim, if one recites Borei Nefashot he will be reciting a blessing in vain, one should follow the majority, in accordance with the words of MB (see below 10:4, note 5). And there is no contradiction in this, for the law of the first blessing depends more on people's perception, whereas the after-blessing depends more on reality, since we give thanks for what we have already eaten and is in the intestines. And we find something similar with rice, over which one recites Mezonot at the beginning and Borei Nefashot at the end.
Over 'leder' (fruit leather) made of apricot that was squashed and completely mashed, into which other flavors that changed its taste were also mixed, one recites Shehakol (Rav Pe'alim 2:28).

sections.title_en: Fruits That Were Completely Mashed, Whose Blessing Is Shehakol
sections.body_en:
Over fruit puree that was mashed by machine (which is commonly fed to babies), one recites Shehakol, for since they underwent complete mashing that changed their form, their blessing changed. And if pieces of fruit remained in the puree, it was not completely mashed, and one recites Ha-etz over the pieces of fruit and thereby exempts the entire puree (Ben Ish Ḥai, Pinḥas 12).

Over regular jam that has no pieces of fruit in it, even though it is known to have been made from fruits, one recites Shehakol. And if pieces of fruit remained in it (confiture), one recites Ha-etz over the pieces of fruit and exempts the rest.

Over tomato paste one recites Shehakol, since they were completely mashed. And although today a great many tomatoes are designated for paste, since the main purpose of tomato paste is to flavor cooked dishes, it has no importance of its own, and since it has changed completely, one who eats it recites Shehakol.

Over Bamba one recites Shehakol; and although it is made from corn flour and peanut butter, since they were completely mashed, its blessing is Shehakol. Likewise over marzipan made of crushed almonds one recites Shehakol.

Over halva or teḥina one recites Shehakol, for since the sesame seeds were completely ground and lost their original form and their name, they also lost their blessing.7

But over a candy made of sesame, sugar and honey, one recites Ha-adama, since most of it is sesame that was not mashed and did not change.

notes_en.en: When a fruit was ground and afterwards another food was created from it, such as millet and corn that were ground and baked into bread, even according to SA 208:8, which rules like the Rambam, one recites Shehakol. The same is the law regarding Bamba and halva, which were first ground and then consolidated again as a new food.

sections.title_en: Sugar, Soy Products and Chocolate – Shehakol
sections.body_en:
Over sugar, whether it was made from sugarcane or from sugar beets, the custom is to recite Shehakol. Admittedly, the great Rishonim disagreed about this, and according to many, since the main purpose of sugarcane and sugar beets is the making of sugar, the blessing over sugar is Ha-adama. However, in practice the custom is to recite Shehakol over it, because sugar has changed so much that it is not at all discernible that it was produced from a fruit of the ground or from sugarcane. And we have already learned that in the laws of blessings we follow people's perception (SA 202:15; MB 76; BHL there).

Likewise over schnitzels, patties and sausages made from soy, the custom is to recite Shehakol. Seemingly it would have been fitting to recite Ha-adama over them, since they are made from soybeans, most of which are grown for grinding and making foods. However, since they were ground and it is not at all discernible that they came from plants, and they look more like meat products, therefore the custom is to recite Shehakol over them. And for the same reason one recites Shehakol over soy cheese.

Likewise over chocolate the custom is to recite Shehakol. Admittedly, some hold that over brown chocolate one recites Ha-etz, since it is made from cocoa beans that grow on a tree, and this is the way they are eaten, and it is even discernible that the chocolate was produced from them, as its color is like the color of cocoa. But as stated, the custom is to recite Shehakol over chocolate, because it has changed greatly from its original form, so that it is not discernible that it came from a fruit. In addition, generally sugar and other ingredients are mixed into chocolate, so that the cocoa is only forty percent of the chocolate.

If one deviated and recited Ha-adama over sugar and soy, or Ha-etz over chocolate, he has fulfilled his obligation (MB 202:76).8

notes_en.en: The basis of the question regarding these three kinds is that we learned in SA 203:7 and 204:11 that a fruit that is usually eaten after grinding, even though it was completely mashed, retains its original blessing. And indeed the Geonim ruled that one recites Ha-adama or Ha-etz over sugar produced from cane. But the custom follows the Rambam, to recite Shehakol over it. BHL 202:15 explained the law regarding sugar beets, that whenever it is not at all discernible that its origin is from a fruit, its blessing is Shehakol. (Regarding sugar produced from cane, there is another reason: that at its beginning it is fruit juice, and as explained below in section 15, their blessing is Shehakol.) The same is the law regarding soy products, in which it is not at all discernible that their origin is from a fruit. Regarding chocolate, there are more doubts, since its color is like the color of the cocoa fruit from which it was produced, and so Minḥat Shlomo 91:2 raised a difficulty. But he too agrees that the custom is to recite Shehakol over it, because … [?]. The reason for the custom is that it changes greatly from its original form, for in addition to its being ground, sugar and other ingredients are also mixed into it; as we have already learned in the law of jam, according to Pri Megadim (202, Mishbetzot Zahav 4) and other Aḥaronim, one recites Shehakol over a fruit that was both mashed and had other ingredients of significance mixed into it. And this is the custom, with the agreement of many of the Aḥaronim.

sections.title_en: Cornflakes, Chips, Falafel Balls, Coconut Candy
sections.body_en:
Over cornflakes made of corn flakes, since the corn was mashed and its appearance changed greatly, one recites Shehakol.

Over French fries (chips) and mashed potatoes made from potatoes, one recites Ha-adama.9

Over falafel balls the custom is to recite Shehakol. And although its main ingredient is chickpeas, and it was not completely mashed, since other ingredients are mixed into it and it is not discernible from its appearance and taste that it is chickpeas, its blessing is Shehakol. And one who recites Ha-adama over it has fulfilled his obligation. One who eats hummus salad, since everyone knows that it is chickpeas and they are grown mainly for this purpose, and its name too remains upon it, recites Ha-adama.

Over coconut candy, which contains a lot of sugar, the custom is to recite Shehakol. And although its mashing is not complete, since a lot of sugar was added to it, and it was also mashed a great deal, it is not perceived as the coconut fruit, and one recites Shehakol over it. All the more so, over coconut cookies one recites Shehakol.

notes_en.en:
Even if the mashed potatoes are mashed a great deal, since people commonly make mashed potatoes from potatoes, and its name and texture remain as before, its blessing is Ha-adama (like the law of homalta; see above, note 3).
Mashed potatoes made from potato flakes (potato flour), since it was completely mashed and its taste also changed slightly, the common ruling is that its blessing is Shehakol. And the common ruling is likewise regarding a chip snack made from potato flour (Pringles), that its blessing is Shehakol. However, one who wishes may recite Ha-adama over them, since according to SA, following the Rambam, in every case their blessing is Ha-adama. And even according to Terumat Ha-deshen, since it is known and discernible that they come from potatoes, it is possible that their blessing is Ha-adama.

sections.body_en:
Over rice, even though it is a kind of legume (kitniyot) that is not one of the five species of grain, the Sages established reciting Mezonot, because it is nourishing like them. But since it is not one of the seven species, after eating it one does not recite a Me'ein Shalosh blessing but only Borei Nefashot (SA 208:7).

This law applies to rice alone, because it is the most similar to grain. But over corn and millet, even though they too are nourishing, and some make bread from them, the Sages did not institute reciting Mezonot. When they were not mashed their blessing is Ha-adama, and when they were ground and made into bread their blessing is Shehakol. And in the countries of South America, where everyone is accustomed to eat corn bread, this is the way corn is eaten, and the blessing over corn bread is Ha-adama (see MB 208:33). Over rice too, only if it was cooked, or kneaded and baked, does one recite Mezonot; but after roasting or slight cooking, one recites Ha-adama (SA 208:7-8).

Regarding rice cakes a doubt arose, because the way they are prepared is not by cooking but by puffing rice grains with heat and sticking them to one another by pressure and heat. And since they have changed greatly, the custom is to recite Shehakol over them.10

Over popcorn, made of corn kernels that puffed up from heat, many wrote to recite Ha-adama, since they did not change as a result of mashing but merely puffed up. And some say to recite Shehakol, and this is the prevalent custom.

notes_en.en: According to Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, Or Le-Tzion 14:21, and Ḥazon Ovadia (Berakhot p. 184) – Ha-adama. According to Rav Elyashiv and Pitḥei Halakha 34 – Mezonot (Sha'arei Ha-berakha 23, 582). According to Rav Eliyahu and Rav Fisher – Shehakol (Ve-zot Ha-berakha pp. 108-109). One may choose, and the custom is to recite Shehakol. Regarding wheat crackers, see 6:13, that one recites Mezonot and Al Ha-miḥya.

sections.body_en:
One who eats a fruit in the way it is customarily eaten, whether raw or cooked, recites its own blessing over it: if it is a fruit of the ground – Ha-adama, and if a fruit of the tree – Ha-etz. And if he ate it not in its usual way, it has lost its stature; but since it is still fit to eat under pressing circumstances, he recites over it the general blessing – Shehakol (SA 205:1; 202:12).

For example, potatoes and squash are usually eaten cooked and not raw. Therefore one who eats them cooked recites Ha-adama, and one who eats them raw, if they are fit to eat under pressing circumstances – recites Shehakol (SA 205:1). But if they are not fit to eat even under pressing circumstances, such as hot pepper and other spices, one does not recite a blessing over them at all (SA 202:16).

Fruits of the tree, such as apples and pears, are usually eaten both raw and cooked; therefore, in both states their blessing is Ha-etz.

There are fruits, such as garlic and onion, that are not usually eaten raw by themselves; rather, they are always secondary to another food, and their role is to give it flavor. Since this is so, they have lost their unique stature as fruit, and one who wishes to eat them raw by themselves should recite Shehakol. But one who cooks or roasts an onion in order to eat it that way should recite Ha-adama over it (based on MB 205:5-7).

Everything depends on local custom. For example, about a hundred years ago it was customary in Europe to eat cabbage only when cooked or pickled, and one who ate it raw would recite Shehakol (MB 205:4). Whereas in the Middle East it was customary to eat it raw as well, and consequently people would recite Ha-adama over it (Kaf Ha-ḥayim 205:8). Today in the Land of Israel, those of Ashkenazic descent too have become accustomed to eat raw cabbage, and therefore the law has changed for them, so that they too recite Ha-adama over it.11

In these laws, even if one erred, he has fulfilled his obligation after the fact. For example, if one should have recited Ha-etz over a cooked fruit, and erred, thinking that this is not the way it is eaten, and recited Shehakol – he has fulfilled his obligation, for over everything, if one recited Shehakol he has fulfilled his obligation. And likewise the reverse: if one ate a raw potato, over which he should have recited Shehakol, since it is not usually eaten raw, and he erred and recited Ha-adama over it – he has fulfilled his obligation, because it is indeed a fruit of the ground (SA 206:1; MB 3).12

notes_en.en: The manner of eating is determined according to what is customary and not according to the possibility of eating. It is a fact that one can eat raw cabbage, and nevertheless, at the time when it was customary in Europe to eat it cooked or pickled, people recited Shehakol over eating it raw (and so wrote MB 205:3). And when people began to eat it raw, its law changed. And even though most still ate it cooked, nevertheless raw too began to be considered an accepted way (BHL 202:10, s.v. "al"). Likewise parsley: in certain places it is customary to eat it by itself without cooking, and consequently its blessing is Ha-adama; and those of Ashkenazic descent are not accustomed to eat it this way, and therefore they should recite Shehakol over it (this is one of the reasons that those of Ashkenazic descent do not eat parsley for karpas on Pesaḥ; see Peninei Halakha: Pesaḥ 16:15).

Sha'arei Teshuva 206:1 wrote that in a case of doubt, it is preferable to recite the more specific blessing, Ha-etz or Ha-adama. However, in practice, in a case of doubt, the ruling is to recite the safer blessing: if the doubt is between Ha-adama and Ha-etz – Ha-adama; and if the doubt is between Ha-adama and Shehakol – Shehakol, as explained in SA 206:1 and Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 205:7, and as I wrote in note 9 [?].

sections.body_en:
Over fruit juices, such as orange juice and carrot juice, one recites Shehakol. Even if they are pure, without any admixture of water, and even if particles of fruit remained in them, since they have changed so much that from a food they have turned into a drink, they have lost their original blessing and received the general blessing – Shehakol. The only fruit that does not descend from its level after it is squeezed is the grape, which after squeezing is elevated to the level of wine, and a special blessing was instituted for it – "Borei peri ha-gafen" (as explained above 7:3).

Even when the juice came out of the fruit naturally, such as honey that oozed from dates, or juice that collected inside a melon, or coconut milk, since it is a drink – one recites Shehakol over it (SA 202:8; Ben Ish Ḥai, Pinḥas 9).

All this applies specifically when the drink has been separated from the fruit; but one who eats the fruit and, while eating it or at the end of eating it, wishes to drink the juice that came out of it – since the drink is secondary to the fruit, it is exempted by its blessing. Therefore, one who eats a grapefruit and recited Ha-etz over it may afterwards drink the juice that collected at the bottom of the plate, because it is secondary to the fruit and is exempted by the Ha-etz blessing he recited over the grapefruit (Ben Ish Ḥai ibid.).13

notes_en.en:
Except for oil and wine, all liquids that come out of fruits have a law different from that of the fruits, both regarding teruma, in that it is forbidden to make fruits that were designated for teruma into liquids [?], and regarding blessings, in that liquids that come out of fruits have the blessing Shehakol, as explained in Berakhot 38a. Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 202:54 explained that the Rishonim disagreed regarding the law of a fruit most of which is grown for squeezing: according to the Rashba the blessing over its juice is Ha-etz, and according to the Rosh, Shehakol; and because of the doubt the halakha follows the Rosh. So ruled SA 205:3; and see Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 205:21 and 202:36. Therefore, even if it turns out that most oranges are grown for squeezing, one recites Shehakol over orange juice. In addition, it is possible that all of the Rashba's words, that we follow the majority, apply only when it is eaten like soup with a spoon, but if it is usually drunk, its blessing is Shehakol. So wrote Tosafot Berakhot 38a, s.v. "hai," at the end, the Gra 202:4, and Igrot Moshe YD vol. 2, end of 25, that over drinking one always recites Shehakol. And so wrote regarding orange juice Or Le-Tzion 14:6, Ḥazon Ovadia (Berakhot p. 125), and Shevet Ha-Levi 4:19.
The after-blessing over pomegranate juice: It seems that today most pomegranates are grown for juice. And although it is a fruit of the seven species, regarding which the doubt is greater, that perhaps its blessing is Al Ha-etz, as explained below in section 17 regarding the liquid of a cooked dish of the seven species, here, where the juice was squeezed, one should recite Borei Nefashot at the end, because perhaps even the Rashba would agree to this, since it is not eaten with a spoon. Furthermore, according to Tosafot, over drinking one always recites Shehakol and Borei Nefashot; and one should also add the opinion of those who hold that the Borei Nefashot blessing exempts, after the fact, those foods requiring the Al Ha-etz blessing (below 10, note 5).

sections.body_en:
One who eats vegetable soup whose main flavor comes from the vegetables in it recites Ha-adama over the vegetables and exempts the rest of the soup. And even if the liquids are the overwhelming majority of the soup and only a few vegetables remain in it, since the flavor of the soup comes from the vegetables, they are the main element, and he recites Ha-adama over them and exempts the liquids. And if the flavor of the soup was created by soup powder and not by the vegetables themselves, the water in the soup is not called vegetable soup, and consequently it is not secondary to the vegetables, and he should recite Ha-adama over the vegetables and Shehakol over the water (see below 11:9, on the law of primary and secondary in soup).

Over clear soup (broth), in any case one recites Shehakol. Even if all its flavor comes from the vegetables and particles of vegetables still remain in it, as long as there are no pieces of vegetable in it that need to be chewed – its blessing is Shehakol. Admittedly, according to most Rishonim, since its flavor comes from vegetables that are usually cooked, its blessing is Ha-adama. However, in practice, since the law is disputed, because of the doubt one recites Shehakol over clear soup.

But over pea, lentil or sweet potato soup, one recites Ha-adama. And although they were mashed until they are not discernible in it, since their substance is evident in the soup, which became thick through them, and it is even called by their name, its blessing is Ha-adama.14

notes_en.en:
One who recites Ha-adama over water recites a blessing in vain; however, over vegetable soup, under certain conditions, one recites Ha-adama. The basis of the discussion is in Berakhot 39a: "The water of all boiled vegetables is like all boiled vegetables." According to the Rosh, the main thing depends on the flavor, and since in cooking the flavor of the vegetable enters the liquids, the blessing over the liquids is like the blessing over the vegetable, on condition that one's intention was to cook the vegetables in order to eat them. According to the Rashba, the law depends on prevalent custom: if it is customary to cook those vegetables, the liquids in the dish too are considered part of the way they are eaten and their blessing is Ha-adama. The Rambam holds like the Rashba, but adds that the purpose of the cooking must also be for the sake of the soup (Kesef Mishneh), and some say that the purpose of the cooking must be solely for the sake of the soup (Arukh Ha-shulḥan). According to all the opinions we have mentioned, under the stated conditions, even if one eats the liquids by themselves he should recite Ha-adama, provided their main flavor is from the vegetables, and this includes even if salt and pepper were added to the soup. But if the soup was cooked with meat as well, since its flavor is more important, the blessing over the soup is Shehakol. So ruled SA 205:2. Likewise, if the soup was flavored with soup powder, and even without the vegetables it would have received the flavor of soup, this soup is not considered vegetable soup, and the blessing over its liquids is Shehakol (see Piskei Teshuvot 205:6).
However, according to the Ra'ah, Ritva and Meiri, only when one eats vegetables together with soup whose flavor comes from them does he recite the blessing over the vegetables and exempt the soup, even though the liquids are the majority, because they are still considered secondary to the vegetables from which their flavor comes. But if he eats the liquids by themselves – he should recite Shehakol. And according to the Maharam, only if the soup became thick because of the vegetables is its blessing Ha-adama. Many of the later Sephardic poskim wrote that one should take into account the approach of the Ra'ah and Ritva, that only if one also eats the vegetables does he exempt the soup with their blessing (Kaf Ha-ḥayim 205:11; Or Le-Tzion vol. 2, 14:31; Ḥazon Ovadia, Berakhot p. 164; and see further Arukh Ha-shulḥan 202:33, 36). Therefore, over clear soup that received its flavor from vegetables one recites Shehakol, and if it contains some vegetables, one recites Ha-adama over the vegetables and thereby exempts the soup as well.
Lentil, pea and sweet potato soup: When, through cooking, the vegetables in it were mashed and made the soup thick, even the Ra'ah and Ritva agree that its blessing is Ha-adama. And one should not say that since they were completely mashed their blessing is Shehakol, for according to the Rambam and many poskim, even when they were completely mashed their blessing is Ha-adama; and in addition, here their name remains upon them, and they are like homalta, as cited in note 3.

sections.body_en:
The law of fruit soup (compote), containing fruits and liquids that were cooked with the fruits, is like the law of vegetable soup. If one eats the fruits with the water, he should recite Ha-etz over the fruits and thereby exempt the water; and even if at the end he is left with water without fruit, he should continue to consume it without reciting Shehakol over it, for it follows after the fruits and is secondary to them.

But if one consumes the soup liquid by itself, the great Rishonim disagreed about this, whether its blessing is Ha-etz or Shehakol. And since there is a doubt about this, one recites Shehakol over it.15

However, if one made juice from a cooked dish of fruits of the seven species, a great problem arises regarding the after-blessing. According to those who hold that one must recite Ha-etz over them at the beginning, their law is like that of fruits of the seven species, and at the end one would have to recite over them one Me'ein Shalosh blessing – Al Ha-etz. And according to those who hold that one must recite Shehakol over them at the beginning, at the end one must recite Borei Nefashot over them. In this case there is no way out, because any blessing he recites at the end will be, according to one of the opinions, a blessing in vain, so it turns out that he cannot recite an after-blessing over this juice. One who wishes to get out of the doubt should drink this juice only within a meal, for Birkat Ha-mazon exempts everything. Or he should eat a food whose blessing is Borei Nefashot, and a fruit of the seven species whose blessing is Al Ha-etz, and with their blessings he will exempt the juice of the fruits of the seven species (SA 202:11).

Over coffee and tea one recites Shehakol; and although their flavor comes from cooking a fruit or leaves, since they are consumed by drinking, one recites Shehakol over them.16

notes_en.en: As explained in note 14; and see SA 202:10-11. And all the more so if one intends to drink them from a cup, their blessing is Shehakol, according to the words of Tosafot Berakhot 38a. And this is the custom. Those who are meticulous try to find a fruit over which to recite Ha-etz and another food over which to recite Shehakol, and have in mind to exempt the liquid of the fruit soup with their blessings.

See note 14. Seemingly there would be room to argue that according to the Rosh, since their flavor comes from cooking the coffee beans and tea leaves, they are the water of boiled produce. And also according to the Rashba, since most of them go to making the drink of coffee and tea, their law is like the water of boiled produce. However, we have already learned that according to the Rosh there is another condition, that the main purpose of the cooking must be for the sake of the fruit, and with tea and coffee one does not eat the fruit. And also with instant coffee the aim is not to eat the fruit but only to flavor the drink. The main reason that one recites Shehakol over them is that the rule accepted in halakha is that over drinking one always recites Shehakol. This is the opinion of Tosafot Berakhot 38a, Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona there, and the Gra 202:4. See above, note 13. And see further SA 204:1 and MB 16, that over barley beer one recites Shehakol, since it is intended for drinking. And see MB 202:34 and Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 36, regarding anigron (a wine-and-oil drink [?]).
